newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ILO said to be ready to help S.Korea over strikes.
newsitem.headline: ILO said to be ready to help S.Korea over strikes.

text.p: South Korea's outlawed umbrella union group said on Thursday the head of the International Labour Organisation had pledged to monitor the country's new labour law and was ready to help the government revise it.

Yoon Young-mo, international spokesman for the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU), and Chung Hae Sook, its vice president, spoke with reporters after holding talks with ILO Director-General Michel Hansenne.

"We appealed to the ILO to remain vigilant and alert and maintain its position until the situation is settled not only to the satisfaction of the Korean people and workers but also to (the satisfaction) of the ILO's own expectations," Yoon said.
The ILO chief was confident the United Nations agency would maintain its monitoring of the controversial law "so it is in compliance with international standards", he told reporters.
"He also said the ILO was willing to be available to the Korean government to work to revise the labour laws and said he would reiterate this openness to the government," Yoon added.
An ILO spokesman confirmed that Hansenne had met the KCTU officials, but declined to give details. However, ILO sources who attended the private talks confirmed Yoon's account.
The Geneva-based agency was set up in 1919 to promote social justice and workers' rights.

South Korean President Kim Young-sam made a dramatic about-face this week to reopen parliamentary debate on the labour law, passed in a dawn session while opposition deputies slept, that has sparked more than three weeks of strikes.
But the Seoul government warned on Thursday it would not tolerate illegal strikes, and the ruling party blasted the opposition for refusing an offer to reopen debate on the law.

Unions argue it undermines workers' rights by giving companies a freer hand to sack employees and replace strikers. The government says flexibility is vital to defend the economy's international competitiveness.
Yoon and Chung said they had thanked Hansenne for his recent letter to Kim, which called on the government to exercise restraint in handling the labour unrest.
The letter, sent on January 10, expressed concern over the threatened arrests of trade union leaders organising strikes. Hansenne has had no reply.
Hansenne said last week there could be no solution to South Korea's worker unrest unless trade union freedom were respected.

The ILO chief was speaking at a news conference at which he announced that the 174-member state body was making a new push this year to have all its members sign up for core labour conventions, including freedom of association for workers.

South Korea joined the ILO in 1991 as it emerged from decades of military rule. It has been reprimanded twice in recent years by the ILO committee on freedom of association, for arrests of trade unionists and non-recognition of trade unions.

In March the committee will meet again and is expected to take up a complaint against South Korea filed by the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), according to ILO and union sources.
